German Automotive Workers Walk Out, Disrupting Production Nationwide

BERLIN, June 12 – Thousands of workers from Germany’s automotive industry staged a walkout on Wednesday, halting production at plants across the country and causing significant disruption to vehicle parts manufacturing. The strike, called by the IG Metall union, focused on demands for higher wages and improved working conditions amid persistent inflation and what union leaders describe as “unprecedented pressures” on staff.

The action began early Wednesday morning, with picket lines forming outside major automotive component factories, including facilities operated by Schaeffler AG, a prominent supplier of bearings and engine parts. By midday, assembly lines at several sites had ground to a halt, prompting concerns among industry leaders about the potential for wider supply chain disruptions.

Schaeffler AG confirmed that operations at its Herzogenaurach and Homburg plants were “severely impacted,” with hundreds of staff participating in the strike. “We respect the right of our employees to voice their concerns,” a spokesperson for Schaeffler AG said. “We are closely monitoring the situation and are committed to finding a swift and constructive resolution with union representatives.”

Other major suppliers, including the Augsburg-based AutoTech Solutions, also reported stoppages, with management estimating a production shortfall of up to 20% if the strike continues into a second day. “We are already seeing delays in order fulfillment for several key customers,” AutoTech Solutions director Petra Neumann said in a statement.

IG Metall, Germany’s largest industrial union, said more than 15,000 workers participated in coordinated walkouts across Bavaria, Baden-Württemberg, and North Rhine-Westphalia. The union is demanding a 7% wage increase, shorter working hours, and assurances on job security as automakers shift production towards electric vehicles and automation.

“Workers have been patient through the transition, but rising costs and restructuring plans have pushed many to the limit,” IG Metall regional secretary Markus Engel told reporters outside a Schaeffler AG plant in Herzogenaurach. “It’s time for companies to recognize the essential role these employees play in maintaining Germany’s competitive edge.”

Industry analysts warned prolonged industrial action could exacerbate existing supply chain bottlenecks, particularly for specialized components. “A strike of this scale in the automotive industry has immediate ripple effects, given the sector’s tight production schedules and just-in-time delivery models,” said Anja Vogel, an industry analyst at the Berlin Institute for Economic Research.

Negotiations between union leaders and employers were ongoing as of Wednesday evening. Both sides expressed hope for a resolution in the coming days, but union officials cautioned further industrial action was possible if demands were not addressed.

The walkout marks the most significant labor unrest in the German automotive sector in over a decade.
